one_line: Astronauts ran 129 burns of small plastic and fabric samples in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS while lowering the oxygen with nitrogen, to find the weakest airflow and the lowest oxygen at which solids keep burning without gravity, and to compare that with the Earth test NASA uses to approve materials.
summary: BASS-II ran 129 burns of small solid samples (126 in 2014, three in 2016) in a 7.6 cm square flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox. Imposed air flows ranged from below 1 to about 55 cm/s. For the first time on ISS the glovebox was diluted with nitrogen, so oxygen ranged from 22.2% to 13.6%. Five teams studied separate configurations: thin PMMA films and thick PMMA slabs in opposed flow, PMMA rods in opposed and concurrent flow, and a cotton-fibreglass fabric in concurrent flow. Thin-film flames went out from radiative loss at about 1 cm/s in air, whatever their thickness, and at 2.6-4 cm/s near 16% O2. The limit fitted for concurrent rod flames has its minimum at about 13.5% O2 (lowest reading with a flame: 13.6%), against a 15.4% upward-burning limit on Earth. Opposed spread over rods persisted to 17.5% O2, against 19% in normal gravity. Fabric flames quenched at 1-5 cm/s. Most flames released under 100 W and burned fuel-rich, producing much CO. Weak ventilation near spacecraft surfaces can therefore sustain flames where Earth tests show none.

question.text: BASS-II tested the same hypothesis as BASS (PSI-26): a material in microgravity with adequate ventilation burns as well as, or better than, the same material in normal gravity at the same pressure, O2 concentration and temperature. NASA screens spacecraft materials with an upward-burning 1 g test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), considered the worst case on Earth, but it may not be conservative in space. BASS-II set out to (1) study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows; (2) bridge the gap between Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and real flammability in microgravity; (3) give preliminary data to refine the science requirements of the follow-on SoFIE project; and (4) use practical, thicker fuels in realistic geometries (slabs, rods, a spherical section, films and fabrics). Many tests looked for the minimum O2 or minimum flow at which a material still burns in space, to compare with Earth-based limits. Others looked at how fast a fire grows and whether the flame reaches a finite size, which matters for firefighting strategy. The new variable compared with BASS was ambient O2, lowered below 21% by adding nitrogen to the glovebox. Despite the project's name, the PSI documents describe no suppression tests in BASS-II; the nitrogen was used only to dilute the atmosphere.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a solid heats the unburnt fuel ahead of it to its pyrolysis temperature. The fuel vapour then mixes with oxygen and burns. In opposed flow (air moving against the spread direction, like downward burning on Earth) the heating comes from a small region at the flame's leading edge. In concurrent flow (air moving with the spread, like upward burning) the whole flame preheats the fuel and can grow. The gas residence time at the leading edge scales as $\alpha_g/V_g^2$. Three regimes follow. At high flow, finite-rate chemistry cannot keep up with the short residence time and the flame blows off (kinetic regime; a small Damkohler number). At moderate flow, the spread rate of a thin fuel is set only by heat conduction and is independent of flow (thermal regime of de Ris). At very low flow, the long residence time lets surface and gas radiation remove a growing fraction of the heat, and the flame quenches (radiative regime). Plotted as O2 against flow, these limits form a U-shaped flammability boundary with a blowoff branch and a quenching branch. On Earth, buoyancy imposes its own flow at the flame: about 0.5 m/s at ignition for the BASS-II rods, and of order 20 cm/s at the base of an upward flame. So the low-flow quenching branch and the bottom of the U, where the minimum oxygen for burning lies, can only be reached in sustained microgravity. For rods and stagnation flames the investigators use a stretch rate $a$ in place of velocity. At about 1-2 cm/s, comparable to a diffusive velocity of 2 cm/s, convection and diffusion supply oxygen at similar rates, and the flame changes from residence-time-limited to diffusion-limited. Thermally thin fuels heat through their whole thickness, so spread rate varies as 1/thickness. Thick fuels such as millimetre PMMA slabs keep a cold core, so ignition and growth are slower and heat loss into the solid and the holder matters.

apparatus.text: The BASS hardware from PSI-26 was reused with new samples, igniters and flash cards. The flow duct was the 7.6 x 7.6 x 17 cm black-anodised duct originally built for SPICE gas-jet flames, installed in the MSG in the ISS Destiny Lab. A variable-speed fan drove air through a honeycomb straightener and an inlet screen. Perforated restrictor plates (0, 1 or 2) on the fan inlet set the range: up to about 55 cm/s with none and about 35 cm/s with two. A TSI 8475 omnidirectional air-velocity transducer measured duct flow. It had a response time of about 1 min and displayed whole cm/s only (about +/-0.5 cm/s). So low flows were set by fan potentiometer and converted using fan calibrations made at the end of each operations day. The fan stops at a finite voltage (above 3.8 V), so the lowest flows sit just above shut-off. An uncalibrated thermopile radiometer (CaF2 window, 0.13-11 um) in the downstream top corner gave a relative flame signal. Samples were lit with Kanthal A-1 29-gauge hot-wire igniters (0.8-1 ohm, 3.5-3.8 A). A Nikon D300s still camera (4,320 x 2,968 pixels, 60 mm lens) looked through the top window at about 1 frame/s. A colour video camera looked through the front window via a mirror; its overlay showed N2 flow, fan voltage, air speed and radiometer. New in BASS-II: the MSG GN2 supply (up to 0.5 L/min through a mass-flow controller) diluted the 250 L glovebox work volume. Before and after each burn, hand-held CSA-CP (O2 at 0.1% resolution, CO 0-1,000 ppm, plus HCl and HCN) and CDM (CO2 0-5%) sensors read the well-mixed work-volume gas. The CSA-CP O2 reading was corrected each day by a constant offset to the ISS Major Constituents Analyzer (MCA). Combustion products left the duct into the sealed work volume, whose filters convert CO to CO2 during the post-test purge.

procedure.text: Each PI had a priority-ordered matrix of about 20 samples, and the ground team directed the crew in real time. For reduced-O2 tests, the crew first flowed GN2 into the closed work volume (MSG air circulation off, BASS fan at maximum) for 25-225 min, as timed by the CSTR dilution model. They recorded CSA-CP and CDM readings before and after each burn. The crew mounted a sample, positioned the igniter within about 1 mm of it, set the flow restrictor and fan, and pulled the igniter lever until a flame appeared; ignition could take up to 60 s in the plan and up to 230 s in practice for rods at low O2. The still camera then ran at about 1 frame/s and the radiometer gain was set. Procedures then differed by sub-investigation. (1) Bhattacharjee: opposed-flow films were ignited at a set flow (mostly 5 cm/s, some 2-10). Flow was then stepped down gradually to radiative extinction, or raised to look for blowoff. Most runs were in air or at about 17% O2, with one at 15%. (2) Miller: thick slabs were burned in opposed flow at 3-20 cm/s for long times, up to about 31 min. Flow was held at plateaus for steady spread and reduced to quenching. O2 was not controlled during a test and drifted down by up to about 3 points as the slab burned. (3) Olson: rods were ignited at the upstream hemispherical tip, typically at 5 cm/s. For quenching limits, the flow was lowered in steps, each held at least about 100 s (the solid response time); tests lasted up to 28 min. For blowoff limits, the flow was raised quickly. Complementary 5.18 s drop-tower blowoff tests were run on the ground. (4) Fernandez-Pello: rods were ignited at the downstream end at high opposed flow. The flow was then reduced in steps, with pauses for steady spread, until extinction. Some tests alternated the fan potentiometer between two settings at 1-2 min intervals to probe the flame's response time. (5) T'ien: fabric was ignited at the leading edge for concurrent spread at 4-11 cm/s, and the flow was often reduced to quenching or raised to blowoff. O2 was fixed by the prior dilution for each test. Partly burned samples were sometimes re-ignited. (6) Ferkul: Nomex was tried in concurrent flow at 8-15 cm/s, and the candle was burned in opposed flow at decreasing flows. After each burn the crew photographed the sample. The work volume was purged for 3 min before access, with further cooling time for touch temperature. The fan was calibrated at the end of each day. Samples were returned to Earth for mass-loss measurements.

psi_data.summary: PSI-25 lists 695 files (274.6 GB). The usable material is small. The 2021 NASA Technical Memorandum (BASS-II Summary Report, TM-20210011385, 141 pages) is the core source: each PI's results, full per-test matrices with crew/PI observations, the dilution model, the anomaly list and a publication list. Also available are the 2010 SRD and hardware manifest, a ReadMe that explains the matrix columns, the per-PI test-matrix workbook, daily fan-calibration data, the crew operations procedure, and the 129-row experimental table with calibrated initial/final O2, CO2 and CO per run. The 125 raw-data 'proof sheets' are downloaded (2,153 text chunks). They hold only per-frame metadata for each still sequence: ISS frame ID, time, shutter, aperture, EV, exposure mode, ISO, and a note on the camera-to-video clock offset. In total about 18,000 frames, mostly 1/3-1/8 s at f/2.0, ISO 1000. The imagery itself is not downloaded: 296 MP4 videos (17.7 GB; downlink, second-view and still-sequence movies) and 264 zips (256.7 GB). The zips are 91 'iss0xxe' crew-camera still archives (135 GB), 58 per-test still zips (96 GB) and 115 'original videos' zips (about 26 GB). findings.claim: Bhattacharjee, thin PMMA films in opposed flow at about 21% O2: flames went out by radiative extinction as the flow was lowered. This happened at about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 um films and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 um (1-2 cm wide, about 1 atm). Within the large uncertainty of flow calibration at such low speeds, the extinction velocity does not depend on thickness, although the spread rate does. A 2-D model gave 1.5 cm/s for all four thicknesses. Approaching extinction, the flame shrank and turned from orange to all blue within about 3 s. With the flow cut off completely, a 100 um flame spreading at 2.2 mm/s went out within 2 s.

sources.quote: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.
Samples were 1- and 2-cm-wide thin films of plastic (PMMA (polymethylmethacrylate)).
However, it must be mentioned that there are significant uncertainties in these values as the calibration at such low velocity has high error bars.
Moreover, the extinction velocity is identical at 1.5 cm/s for all the four thicknesses studied.

After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s, as shown by the radiometer signal drop in Figure 2.2.

The as-run log records high-flow blowoff of 100 and 200 um films at about 17.4% O2 (fan potentiometer 6.0-7.0), whereas two film runs at about 21% O2, with the fan raised to its maximum setting (air display about 10 cm/s), kept spreading without blowing off.

findings.claim: Bhattacharjee: across opposed flows from about 40 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s in microgravity, the highest spread rate over 100 um PMMA (2 cm wide, about 20.7-21% O2) was 2.2 mm/s. This is about the same as the 2.0 mm/s measured for downward spread in 1 g air on the same fuel, and the flame shapes were similar. The authors conclude that downward spread over PMMA at 21% O2 on Earth is thermally controlled with little kinetic effect. Applying the de Ris thin-fuel formula to the 2.2 mm/s maximum spread rate for 100 um film gives F = 4.76. Combined with 1 g thick-fuel data (0.044 mm/s), this gives an effective buoyant opposed velocity of 1.9 cm/s and a thin/thick transition thickness of 5.2 mm for downward spread in air.

This indicates that at 21 percent O2 level, downward spread over PMMA can be considered thermally controlled with minimal kinetic effect.

findings.claim: Olson, PMMA rods (0.318-0.635 cm radius) ignited at the upstream tip in axial stagnation (concurrent) flow: the ISS tests traced a U-shaped flammability boundary in O2 against stretch rate, with a quenching branch at low stretch and a linear blowoff branch at high stretch. Its minimum is about 13.5% O2 at a = 8-12 1/s (about 1.7-2.5 cm/s for the 0.318 cm radius rod). This is well below the 15.4% O2 upward-burning limit measured in 1 g with an extra 4 cm/s forced flow, so the material stays flammable in the weak ventilation that only microgravity provides. The lowest sustained flame (0.476 cm radius rod) quenched at a final reading of 13.6% O2, from a start of 14.8%. Blowoff limits from 5.18 s drop-tower tests agreed with the ISS data. Because the blowoff branch is linear, the authors propose extrapolating 1 g blowoff limits to zero stretch as a conservative estimate of the minimum O2 for flammability in space; ground tests later found the 1 g mixed-convection blowoff boundary also linear.

The fact that the blowoff boundary is linear with flow makes it possible to extrapolate blowoff data down to zero a and use that O2 value as an accurate but conservative estimate of the minimum O2 concentration for material flammability in space.
From these results, the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed.

findings.claim: Olson: the ignition limit lies above the extinction limit. Below about 14.5% initial O2, no sustained flame could be ignited (a 0.476 cm radius rod at 13.6% O2 did not ignite at any flow), yet flames lit at higher O2 survived down to 13.6%. Ignition delay was within about 40 s at higher O2 but rose sharply below 16% O2, to as long as 230 s for the larger rods, because heat is lost into the cold rod. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 uses a fixed igniter time of about 25 s, and BASS-II ignition delays were up to almost 10 times longer. The authors suggest that Test 1 may therefore act as an ignition test rather than a flammability test at near-limit conditions.

findings.claim: Olson, rod extinction mechanisms and energy balance. Near quenching, the flame shrank to a blue hemisphere (length/width about 0.5). Its open tail leaked fuel, and the radiometer showed oscillations at a steady 1.1 Hz with growing amplitude before extinction, like quiescent candle flames in microgravity. Blowoff began as a hole in the flame at the stagnation point. Once the hole moved more than about one thermal length (about 2 mm) downstream, the flame could not move back upstream even when the flow was reduced; in one of two attempts it did re-close within 7 s. A surface energy balance using a critical Damkohler number shows fuel vaporisation taking about 70% of the flame heat flux on the blowoff branch, falling to 20% on the quenching branch. At the lowest stretch, losses (mostly surface radiation) exceed 60%. Gas radiative feedback rises from 1% to over 13% of the surface heating. The switch from blowoff to quenching occurs where the forced flow equals a diffusive velocity of about 2 cm/s.

sources.quote: Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out. Blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.
The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz as shown in the inset to Figure 6.6

Once the stagnation region is blown far enough downstream of the stagnation region (greater than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ), the flame is unable to propagate back upstream even when the flow is reduced.
It is interesting that across the entire blowoff branch, the vaporization ratio is ~70 percent, whereas it drops precipitously to 20 percent at low a along the quenching branch.
At the lowest a, the total heat loss fraction exceeds 60 percent of the total flame to surface feedback.
The transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the forced-flow velocity becomes the same order as the diffusive velocity (U/UD = 1) for this geometry.

findings.claim: Fernandez-Pello and Link, opposed-flow spread over black PMMA rods (6.35-12.7 mm diameter) at 16.8-20.9% O2 and forced flows of a few mm/s to a few cm/s: spread rate rose with opposed flow and with O2, and thinner rods spread faster. The flames were small, blue, faint and open-tailed at the lowest flows, and luminous, yellow and closed-tipped above about 2 cm/s. No sustained spread was seen below about 4 mm/s for the 6.35 and 9.525 mm rods. In microgravity, spread was sustained down to 17.5% O2, against 19% in 1 g, and was appreciably faster than in 1 g. The related journal paper (flows 0.4-8 cm/s, O2 15-21%) reports that spread rate first rises then falls as opposed flow increases, and gives 17% vs 18% for the lowest O2 sustaining spread in microgravity vs 1 g; these figures differ from the 17.5% vs 19% in the NASA TM.

sources.quote: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 0.00635- and 0.009525-m- diameter rods.
As the flow velocity rises towards 20 mm/s and above, the flames become much more luminous, with bright yellow flames, and a closed downstream tip.
While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
It is also apparent that flame spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1g for cylindrical rods of PMMA.
Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments, as shown in Figure 4.3.
The data show that as the opposed flow velocity is increased, the flame spread rate first increases, and then decreases, different from that on Earth.
Results also show that flame spread in microgravity could be faster and sustained at lower oxygen concentration (17%) than in normal gravity (18%).

findings.claim: Rods at low O2 (Fernandez-Pello and Olson): at 16.3% O2 and 5 cm/s, a black PMMA rod held a cap-shaped flame on its tip. The flame burned the hemispherical tip flat, then went out, and never spread along the rod. Olson notes that opposed-flow spread over rods was not observed below 16.4% O2 at any flow. Post-burn rods show bubble layers of methyl methacrylate vapour that burst as vapour jets. Hot material keeps producing fuel after extinction, and concurrent-rod flame oscillations persisted longer than in 1 g. The authors therefore recommend continuing spacecraft fire suppression until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapour.

sources.quote: The flame survived under the low-O2 conditions until the initially hemispherical rod tip regressed to a flat surface. It never spread along the outer surface of the rod.

This is consistent with tests for opposed-flow flame spread over rods that were also done as part of BASS–II (Ref. 14), where opposed-flow flame spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.
After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools.
This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.

findings.claim: T'ien, SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric in concurrent flow (1.2 and 2.2 cm wide, 16.4-20.8% O2, about 1 atm): 27 BASS-II tests, of which six reached quenching, three did not ignite and one blew off. Quenching flow speeds were 1-5 cm/s, higher at lower O2. This traces the low-speed quenching branch of the concurrent-spread flammability boundary, which the authors call the first such boundary determined cleanly; it agrees qualitatively with earlier theory. Near quenching the flame shrank in length and width to a circular blue flame and went out three-dimensionally. The 2.2 cm fabric did not ignite at 16.4% O2 (5 and 10 cm/s) or 16.8% O2 (5 cm/s). A 1.2 cm sample at 17.2% O2 blew off when the flow was raised from 11 to about 47 cm/s, while a 2.2 cm sample at 16.9% O2 did not blow off at 53 cm/s. The narrow samples had a smaller flammable domain, but their quenching limit was not resolved.

The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower O2 atmosphere.
This is the first time that a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread is determined in a clean and unambiguous manner.

findings.claim: Ferkul: all three Nomex III fabric samples failed to sustain a flame in concurrent flow at 21.0-22.2% O2 and 8-15 cm/s; they flashed briefly or went out while the igniter was still on. The authors call this an excellent result for ISS, where Nomex is used as a fire barrier. The leftover BASS Japan-wax candle, at 17.4% O2 in opposed flow, had a long ignition and then burned at five decreasing flows from 3 cm/s. The flame went from long and sooty to hemispherical to short and mostly blue before going out at the lowest potentiometer setting (0.305). It ejected a wax droplet upstream, illustrating that low-viscosity melts can carry burning droplets to other materials in microgravity.

findings.claim: Combustion products, all PMMA tests: before-and-after sensor readings showed O2 consumed against CO2 produced following the 6:5 stoichiometric ratio for PMMA over all geometries, flows and initial O2. CO per CO2 depended on geometry. Concurrent rods gave on average about 550 ppm CO per 1% CO2 (about 600 ppm in the rod-only analysis), and opposed thick slabs about 370 ppm. Opposed rods were strongly nonlinear. CO/CO2 ratios were mostly well above the 0.004 typical of efficient combustion, and for concurrent rods rose as O2 fell. O2-consumption calorimetry (13.1 kJ/g O2) puts most flames well below 100 W; the highest were about 100 W for a long thick-slab burn and about 110 W for a concurrent rod. Mass loss of 19 returned samples against O2 consumed gives a global equivalence ratio of about 1.3, so the flames were fuel-rich and released unburnt fuel, soot and CO. Rod flames were near-stoichiometric at high O2 and grew richer near the limit. The authors estimate that a BASS-II-sized fire mixed into the 106 m3 US Lab would raise CO by only about 1.5 ppm, below the 10 ppm long-term spacecraft maximum allowable concentration. The CO sensor saturated (over 1,000 ppm) in several low-O2 rod tests.

sources.quote: As shown, the data agrees very well with stoichiometric ratios for the wide range of test conditions.
Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
The opposed thick slabs fall somewhere in between, producing on average 370 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.

For efficiently burned flue gases (boilers, furnaces, etc.), this ratio is typically less than 0.004. As can be seen, most of our data is well above that, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.

The one long opposed thick slab test that caused the lower downstream corner of the front window damage released close to 100 W. A prior relatively brief concurrent rod test that released almost 110 W did not cause any damage.
we can use the above equations to solve for the effective equivalence ratio for the tests: Φglobal = 1.3, which is fuel rich.

findings.claim: Ground blowoff tests on the BASS-II rod geometry in 1 g (cast PMMA rods of 0.318-1.905 cm radius, 14-18% O2, upward axial stagnation flow in a 7.6 cm tube) gave a linear blowoff boundary that runs parallel to the BASS-II microgravity boundary but at lower forced stretch. Shifting the 1-g boundary by a buoyant stretch of about 78 1/s, equivalent to a forced flow of about 16.5 cm/s for the base rod and consistent with buoyant-velocity estimates, brings the two into agreement. The authors propose measuring the 1-g blowoff boundary, adding the buoyant stretch and extrapolating to zero stretch as a ground estimate of microgravity flammability limits. Whether the buoyant-stretch constant holds for other materials is untested.

sources.quote: The normal gravity blowoff boundary was parallel to the BASS-II boundary, but shifted to lower stretch rates.

In order to account for the additional inherent buoyant stretch, the normal gravity boundary was empirically shifted to the right by a value ab =78 s-1, which for the base rod size corresponds to a forced flow velocity of 16.5 cm/s, in good agreement with buoyant flow velocity estimates.
Further research is needed to determine the applicability of the buoyant stretch constant K for different materials.

relevance.text: Prevention and material screening: BASS-II gives direct evidence that, at about 1 atm, microgravity with weak ventilation can be more hazardous than the 1 g screening configuration. The limit fitted for concurrent PMMA rod flames has its minimum at about 13.5% O2 (lowest reading with a flame: 13.6%), against a 15.4% upward limit in 1 g. Opposed spread over rods persisted to 17.5% O2, against 19% in 1 g, and was faster. Ignition at near-limit O2 took up to about 230 s, against the roughly 25 s igniter time of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, so a material that 'passes' by not igniting may still burn once lit. The dangerous range of flows (about 1-10 cm/s, around the minimum of the U-shaped boundary) is, in the authors' words, typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces. Two practical routes to Earth-based derating come out of the work: extrapolating the linear 1 g blowoff boundary to zero stretch (Olson), and using the de Ris thermal-regime correlation validated in microgravity (Bhattacharjee). For response: in these tests, low-flow flames were extinguished by cutting the ventilation, but hot thermoplastics keep releasing vapour and can eject burning droplets, so suppression should continue until the material has cooled. Nomex III did not sustain a flame in air, which supports its use as a fire barrier. Atmosphere: small (under 100 W), fuel-rich microgravity flames produced CO/CO2 ratios an order of magnitude above efficient combustion. Over 1,000 ppm CO built up in the 250 L glovebox, though dilution into a large module would keep CO low. Limits on transferability: all results are for PMMA, a cotton-fibreglass fabric and Nomex, in a small duct at about 1 atm and 13.6-22.2% O2. They are configuration-specific limits, not certified material ratings.

habitat_conditions.text: BASS-II ran at ISS cabin pressure: about 1 atm, with 99.2-99.5 kPa reported for the film tests. O2 ranged from 22.2% down to 13.6% (calibrated readings), close to the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa) and below it. It therefore covers normoxic and hypoxic atmospheres at sea-level pressure only. It does not reach the proposed Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less) or the 100% O2 / 29.6 kPa suit atmosphere. In those, the O2 partial pressure and mole fraction are higher, and the lower density changes residence times and the buoyant and diffusive velocities. The BASS-II limits (e.g. 13.5% O2 minimum for rods, 1-5 cm/s quenching speeds for fabric) are thus lower-bound reference points; they are not limits for exploration atmospheres. The investigators themselves list low pressure and elevated O2 among expected spacecraft conditions, but did not test them. The flow range (below 1 to about 55 cm/s) spans spacecraft ventilation speeds and near-quiescent pockets.

Fire safety is a concern in space travel, particularly with the current plans of increasing the length of the manned space missions, and of using spacecraft atmospheres different than in Earth, such as microgravity, low-velocity gas flow, low pressure and elevated oxygen concentration.

earth_benefits.text: Buoyancy-free data with simple flow fields validate combustion models: the 2-D opposed-spread model, the de Ris correlation, the 3-D transient concurrent-spread model and FDS. These models can then be extended to buoyant flames on Earth, such as wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion. The microgravity film data showed that downward spread over PMMA in air on Earth is thermally controlled. They also gave a de Ris coefficient and a thin/thick transition thickness of about 5.2 mm usable in terrestrial fire modelling. The work also feeds normal-gravity surrogate test methods: the narrow-channel apparatus (Miller) and the zero-stretch blowoff extrapolation (Olson).

sources.quote: Detailed combustion models can be validated by data obtained in the simpler flow environment in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity.
For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.
So, the BASS–II results will be used in comparison with ground-based experimental setups aimed at replacing NASA’s current test method for screening materials used onboard spacecraft.

limitations.text: Flow is poorly known exactly where the limits lie. The air-velocity transducer responds in about 1 min and reads only whole cm/s. The lowest flows were set by fan potentiometer near the fan's shut-off voltage, and in the logs they are recorded as settings (e.g. pot 0.30-0.36) rather than speeds. Daily calibrations were sometimes incomplete, and flow takes time to reach the flame after a change. Bhattacharjee warns of large error bars, and Olson notes the uncertainty below 1 cm/s on the quenching branch.

limitations.text: Few tests per condition and repeated use of samples. Each PI had about 20 samples spread over several variables, for example only two film tests at about 16% O2, with different widths. Many samples were re-ignited, cut or had their igniter leads removed, which changes geometry and pre-heating (one rod re-burn quenched at a markedly lower flow than the first burn). Ignition was manual, with variable igniter placement and timing.
